title: Enteric fever: typhoid and paratyphoid (international guidance)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Take blood cultures before antibiotics and a detailed travel history. Avoid empirical fluoroquinolones. Uncomplicated: oral azithromycin. Complicated: IV ceftriaxone, or a carbapenem if acquired in Pakistan or Iraq (XDR risk). Tailor to susceptibility, give dexamethasone for severe typhoid with encephalopathy or shock, and follow public health clearance rules.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Incubation 6 to 30 days for typhoid and 1 to 10 days for paratyphoid. Insidious fatigue and fever rising to 39 to 40°C by day 3 or 4, with headache, anorexia, abdominal pain, and constipation or diarrhoea.

Complications affect 10 to 15% of hospitalised patients, usually after 2 to 3 weeks of illness: gastrointestinal bleeding, intestinal perforation and encephalopathy. Mortality is under 1% with prompt treatment and above 10% untreated.

Most imported cases follow travel to South Asia. Since 2016 extensively drug-resistant (XDR) S. Typhi from Pakistan is resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole, ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone but susceptible to azithromycin and carbapenems (CDC; XDR also reported from Iraq).
Always record the countries visited and dates: the travel history drives empirical therapy while cultures are pending.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Blood cultures before antibiotics: a single culture is positive in only about 50%, so take more than one. Bone marrow culture is about 80% sensitive and stays positive after antibiotics. Send stool culture too.
Do not use the Widal test or other antibody tests to diagnose or exclude enteric fever: they cannot separate current from past infection or vaccination.
Request full antimicrobial susceptibility testing (including ceftriaxone, azithromycin and fluoroquinolones) and adjust treatment to it.
CBC, liver enzymes, creatinine and electrolytes; malaria testing in travellers from endemic areas; urgent imaging and surgical review for abdominal pain, distension or peritonism.

sections.title: Uncomplicated enteric fever
items: Do not use fluoroquinolones empirically: most S. Typhi and Paratyphi A are fluoroquinolone non-susceptible, with treatment failure (CDC).
Travel to Pakistan or Iraq: azithromycin orally. Other destinations: azithromycin or ceftriaxone remain appropriate empirical choices (CDC).
Azithromycin: adults 1 g orally once daily; children 20 mg/kg once daily (maximum 1 g), for 7 days. Check the QTc when other QT-prolonging drugs are used.
Once susceptibilities are known, a narrower agent (for example a fluoroquinolone for a fully susceptible isolate) may be used on specialist advice.

Fever commonly persists for 3 to 5 days on effective treatment while the daily maximum falls; do not switch for fever alone. Fever beyond 5 days: review susceptibility and look for an abscess, bone, joint or other focal infection.

sections.title: Complicated or severe enteric fever
items: No XDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily in adults (children 50 to 80 mg/kg once daily, maximum 2 g). Travel to Pakistan or Iraq (XDR risk): a carbapenem such as meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly (children 20 mg/kg 8-hourly, maximum 1 g) until susceptibilities are known.
Adding oral or IV azithromycin to the IV agent is common practice in severe disease or when the response is slow.
Switch to an oral agent to which the isolate is susceptible once afebrile and eating, completing usually 10 to 14 days in total for complicated disease.
Severe typhoid with delirium, obtundation, stupor, coma or shock: dexamethasone 3 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes, then 1 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 8 doses.
Intestinal perforation: resuscitate, nil by mouth, urgent laparotomy, and add anaerobic cover (for example metronidazole 500 mg IV 8-hourly) unless on a carbapenem. Steroids can mask peritonism.

sections.title: Follow-up, relapse and carriage
items: Relapse occurs in up to 10% of patients 1 to 3 weeks after clinical recovery; re-culture and retreat according to susceptibility.
1 to 4% of treated patients become chronic carriers (stool excretion for 12 months or more); carriers need specialist-directed prolonged eradication therapy and public health follow-up.

Notify public health. UKHSA risk groups (people unable to maintain hygiene, children aged 5 or under in childcare, food handlers, and health, social care or nursery staff) are excluded until 3 consecutive negative faecal samples taken at least 48 hours apart, starting 1 week after antibiotics finish.
Others are excluded only while symptomatic and until 48 hours symptom-free. Co-travellers in risk groups give one faecal sample; for non-travel cases screen all household and close contacts.

sections.title: Children, pregnancy and national policy
items: Children: azithromycin orally or ceftriaxone IV by weight; meropenem for suspected XDR infection.
Pregnancy: ceftriaxone or azithromycin; avoid fluoroquinolones and chloramphenicol; meropenem if XDR infection is suspected.
India: ICMR and IAP guidance also allows cefixime for uncomplicated disease; international guidance prefers azithromycin, and fluoroquinolone resistance is widespread in South Asian isolates.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV): single injectable dose from 6 months of age up to 45 or 65 years depending on the product (WHO); more effective in young children and longer lasting than older vaccines.

Vi polysaccharide vaccine 0.5 mL IM from 2 years of age, booster every 2 years if risk continues (CDC); oral Ty21a 4 capsules on alternate days from 6 years, booster every 5 years. Both protect 50 to 80% of recipients.
No vaccine prevents paratyphoid: safe food and water and hand hygiene remain essential for all travellers, vaccinated or not.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Starting antibiotics before blood cultures are taken.
Diagnosing or excluding typhoid on a Widal test.
Empirical ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone alone for a severely ill traveller from Pakistan.
Changing antibiotics for fever that has not yet had 5 days to settle.
Missing perforation in an obtunded patient or one on dexamethasone.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.dose: Adults 1 g orally once daily; children 20 mg/kg once daily (maximum 1 g); 7 days
drugs.notes: First-line oral agent, including XDR infection. QTc caution with interacting drugs.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: Adults 2 g IV once daily; children 50 to 80 mg/kg IV once daily (maximum 2 g)
drugs.notes: Complicated disease without XDR risk; total course usually 10 to 14 days including oral step-down.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.dose: Adults 1 g IV every 8 hours; children 20 mg/kg every 8 hours (maximum 1 g per dose)
drugs.notes: Complicated disease acquired in Pakistan or Iraq (XDR risk). Reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.dose: 3 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes, then 1 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 8 doses
drugs.notes: Severe typhoid with encephalopathy (delirium, obtundation, coma) or shock.

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.notes: Added for intestinal perforation when not on a carbapenem.
